common_name: Marshall's Seedless Ash (Marshall Seedless Green Ash)

planting.note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container-grown grafted stock in early fall or early spring in any moist, well-drained soil in full sun; this seedless male clone must be propagated by grafting or budding onto seedling rootstock rather than grown from seed.

directions: Marshall's Seedless was one of the first fruitless (all-male) selections of green ash introduced to commerce in the 1950s, prized for its glossy dark-green summer foliage, clean yellow fall color, and freedom from the messy seed litter of wild seedling trees. Its vigorous, uniform growth and adaptability to compacted, salty, and alkaline urban soils made it one of the most widely planted street and boulevard trees in the American Midwest and Great Plains through the late 20th century. That very ubiquity became a cautionary tale in the emerald ash borer era: because so many cities planted this single clone as a monoculture along entire streets, EAB has been able to wipe out whole blocks of urban canopy at once. New plantings should only be considered where active EAB monitoring or biocontrol programs are in place, and always mixed with other genera to avoid repeating the same monoculture mistake.
sources: USDA Forest Service Silvics of North America

planting.note: Plant grafted, balled-and-burlapped or container stock in early fall or early spring in any well-drained soil in full sun; Patmore is exceptionally cold-hardy and widely grown on the northern Great Plains and Canadian prairies where few large shade trees thrive.

directions: Patmore is a seedless (male), cold-hardy selection of green ash that originated in Alberta and became a mainstay street and shelterbelt tree across the Canadian prairies and northern Great Plains, where its reliable survival of extreme winter cold set it apart from other ash cultivars bred in milder nurseries. It grows into a strongly upright oval crown with a dominant central leader, needing less corrective pruning than many ash selections, and produces clean, dark-green foliage without the litter of a seed-bearing tree. As with all ash cultivars, its future in the landscape depends entirely on regional emerald ash borer management; plant it only where active monitoring or treatment programs make long-term survival realistic, and never as a single-species street planting.

planting.note: Plant grafted, balled-and-burlapped or container stock in early fall or early spring in any moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Summit forms a strong central leader with minimal formative pruning needed.

directions: Summit is a seedless green ash selection valued for its distinctly upright, pyramidal-to-oval habit with a strong central leader, a more uniform silhouette than the broader-spreading wild species and one that requires less structural pruning over the tree's life. Its clean dark-green foliage turns a good yellow in fall and it shares the parent species' tolerance of clay soils, urban compaction, and brief flooding. Like all green ash cultivars, Summit is highly susceptible to emerald ash borer, so it should be planted only in areas with an active regional EAB management program and always interplanted with other tree genera rather than used as a monoculture street tree.

planting.note: Plant grafted, balled-and-burlapped or container stock in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; this seedless male clone must be propagated by grafting rather than grown from seed.

directions: Autumn Purple is a seedless (male) selection of white ash chosen for its unusually reliable, long-lasting fall display — the large compound leaves turn a deep, uniform maroon-purple weeks before most seedling white ash trees color, and the display persists longer than on the species. It shares white ash's large, rounded canopy and moderate growth rate, making it a substantial shade tree for parks, campuses, and large residential lots rather than a compact yard tree. As with all Fraxinus selections, Autumn Purple is highly vulnerable to emerald ash borer, and planting should be limited to regions with active EAB biocontrol or treatment programs, ideally mixed among other canopy species rather than planted as a single-genus row.

planting.note: Plant grafted, balled-and-burlapped or container stock in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Autumn Applause forms a tighter, more rounded crown than seedling white ash and needs comparatively little formative pruning.

directions: Autumn Applause is a seedless white ash selection with a denser, more compact oval-to-rounded crown than the wide-spreading species, making it a better fit for street tree lawns and medium-sized residential properties. Its dark green summer foliage turns an early, reddish-purple fall color, generally coloring up a week or two ahead of typical seedling white ash trees. Being a Fraxinus americana clone, it carries the same near-total vulnerability to emerald ash borer as the species; plant it only where regional EAB management is active, and pair it with a diverse mix of other genera to avoid recreating a single-species canopy.
sources: J. Frank Schmidt & Son Co. — Journal

planting.note: Plant grafted, balled-and-burlapped or container stock in early spring in any well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Prairie Pride tolerates compacted urban soils, heat, and drought as well as wild-type hackberry.

directions: Prairie Pride is a selected clone of common hackberry chosen for a more symmetrical, uniformly rounded crown than the often irregular wild-seedling species, along with glossier dark-green foliage and improved resistance to the witches'-broom growth distortion that disfigures many hackberry trees over time. It retains the outstanding adaptability of the species — tolerating compacted urban soils, drought, heat, wind, and air pollution — while producing a more predictable, landscape-ready form for street tree and shade tree plantings. Its small dark berries still ripen in fall and provide the same wildlife value as the species, feeding numerous songbirds and supporting hackberry emperor and other Celtis-dependent butterflies.
sources: J. Frank Schmidt & Son Co. — Journal

planting.note: Plant grafted, balled-and-burlapped or container stock in fall or spring in any well-drained soil in full sun; Shademaster is thornless and produces few if any seed pods, unlike the wild species.

directions: Shademaster is a thornless, essentially podless selection of honeylocust with a vigorous, upright-spreading habit and ascending branches that form a strong central leader — a more disciplined shape than the sprawling wild species. Its fine-textured, twice-compound leaflets cast the same light, dappled shade typical of honeylocust, allowing lawns and underplantings to succeed beneath the canopy, and the foliage holds its dark green color later into fall than many other cultivars before dropping with little raking required. Shademaster inherited the species' exceptional tolerance of alkaline soil, compaction, salt spray, heat, and drought, making it one of the most dependable large shade trees for difficult street and parking-lot plantings.
sources: USDA Forest Service Silvics of North America

planting.note: Plant grafted, balled-and-burlapped or container stock in fall or spring in any well-drained soil in full sun; Skyline develops a strong central leader and pyramidal young form, broadening with age.

directions: Skyline is a thornless, nearly podless honeylocust selection prized for a distinctly pyramidal young form with a dominant central leader, broadening into a wide-spreading, flat-topped crown as the tree matures. Its fine, feathery compound foliage emerges later in spring than many trees and turns a clear golden-yellow in fall, casting the light, dappled shade characteristic of the species without heavy leaf litter. Skyline carries the same tolerance of alkaline, compacted, salty, and drought-prone urban soils as other inermis selections, making it a long-standing favorite for street tree plantings, parking lot islands, and other difficult sites where few large trees perform reliably.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Plant grafted, balled-and-burlapped or container stock in fall or spring in any well-drained soil in full sun; Sunburst is more prone to twig dieback and canker than other honeylocust cultivars, so avoid stressed or poorly drained sites.

directions: Sunburst is a smaller, thornless honeylocust selection grown for its striking new growth — each flush of foliage emerges bright golden-yellow before fading to green over the summer, giving the whole canopy a two-toned glow that is especially vivid in spring and after a midsummer pruning flush. Its more modest mature size and lighter, rounder crown suit smaller residential lots better than the larger inermis cultivars, while still providing the species' characteristic fine-textured, dappled shade. Sunburst is more susceptible to twig and branch cankers than other honeylocust selections, so it performs best with good air circulation, well-drained soil, and avoidance of drought or winter-injury stress that can invite dieback.

planting.note: Plant grafted, balled-and-burlapped or container stock in fall or spring in any well-drained soil in full sun; Imperial's compact, rounded form fits smaller residential lots and tree lawns better than larger honeylocust cultivars.

directions: Imperial is a compact, thornless honeylocust selection with a broadly rounded, low-branching crown that stays smaller than most inermis cultivars, making it one of the better honeylocust choices for narrow street tree lawns and modest residential yards. Its fine, feathery compound leaves produce the same light, filtered shade typical of the species, allowing turf and underplantings to thrive beneath it, and the foliage turns clear yellow before dropping with minimal cleanup. Imperial retains the species' strong tolerance of alkaline soils, compaction, heat, and drought, giving it the same reliability as larger honeylocust cultivars in tough urban planting sites while requiring less overhead clearance.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Plant grafted, balled-and-burlapped or container stock in fall or spring in any well-drained soil in full sun; Moraine develops a broad, wide-spreading crown and benefits from early structural pruning to establish a strong central leader.

directions: Moraine is among the earliest thornless honeylocust selections brought into commerce, valued for a broad, wide-spreading, vase-shaped crown and for producing few if any of the large twisted seed pods that litter the ground under wild honeylocust trees. Its fine, airy compound foliage casts the light, dappled shade the species is known for, letting grass and groundcovers grow well beneath a mature canopy, and the leaves turn soft yellow before dropping in fall with little raking needed. Like other inermis selections, Moraine tolerates alkaline soil, compaction, heat, drought, and urban stress with ease, and its long track record in cultivation makes it a proven choice wherever a large, wide-canopied shade tree is needed.
sources: USDA Forest Service Silvics of North America
